ch09 - Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing.md
chapters.relation: The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.

chapters.file: ch10 - I So We Bailed on That Reality and We Came to This One.md
ch11 - 1. The Genuine Article.md
chapters.relation: Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.

chapters.file: ch12 - 2. The Unimportance of Identity When You Have a Portal Gun.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.

chapters.file: ch13 - 3. The M. Night Sh-imulation Hypothesis.md
chapters.relation: The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.

chapters.file: ch14 - 4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk.md
chapters.relation: Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.

chapters.file: ch15 - 5. Who’d Rick Kill Or, Who Killed Rick.md
chapters.relation: Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.

chapters.file: ch16 - 6. Truth in a Multiverse.md
chapters.relation: Expanding outward from Rick's garage to define a 'world' as everything spatiotemporally connected, the chapter explains truth via the correspondence theory (claims are true when they match actual events, like the 2016 election) and the coherence theory (for truths like googol arithmetic that correspond to nothing). It argues that in Rick and Morty's world possible worlds are not abstract tools but real alternate timelines: Beth really could have been a human doctor and Jerry really could have been on DiCaprio's yacht, as 'Rixty Minutes' shows, and the Cronenberg timeline's brave Jerry proves a non-weenie Jerry is possible. Yet infinite timelines may still miss possibilities (Jerry's favorite even number), so abstract possible worlds keep a role, with David Lewis the lone real-world philosopher who took them as actually existing.

chapters.file: ch17 - II Come Watch TV.md
ch18 - 7. Rick and Morty as Socratic Television.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Harmon and Roiland write the show as Socratic dialogue: in 'Mortynight Run' Morty's confident moral position (saving Fart from Krombopulos Michael is right) is dismantled until Morty himself pulls the trigger, leaving him in aporia; in 'Auto Erotic Assimilation' Summer's faith in freedom is razed by Unity's happy paternalist hive and the nipple-shaped race war it unleashes; and 'Look Who's Purging Now' refuses to choose between liberalism and conservatism when the post-purge town instantly re-founds the Festival. Like Socrates in Plato's Meno, the show's goal is not to teach lessons but to reduce viewers to confusion, because doing philosophy begins there.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need.md
chapters.relation: Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.

chapters.file: ch20 - 9. The Fallacy of the Many Heads.md
chapters.relation: The chapter uses Headism in 'Get Schwifty' as a case study in illusory correlation: Principal Vagina walks out to pray just as the Cromulons approve of Rick and Morty's song, so the town builds a false cause-and-effect religion from coincidence, compounding false positives until Beth and Jerry are nearly sacrificed to the Giant Heads. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's System 1/System 2 model and Peter Wason's confirmation-bias studies, it argues the characters reason rationally on the information available but never check whether their information is sufficient, the same lazy thinking that sustains religious faith, ghost photos, and the Loch Ness Monster. The cure is effortful skepticism, stopping to ask whether we might be wrong, lest we end up shooting Mr. Poopybutthole.

chapters.file: ch21 - 10. On Being and Meeseeks.md
chapters.relation: The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.

chapters.file: ch22 - 11. Are You Imagining That Poopybutthole.md
chapters.relation: Reading 'Total Rickall' as an evil-genius scenario, the chapter treats the memory parasites (Uncle Steve, Sleepy Gary, Reverse Giraffe) as Descartes's deceiving demon lodged in the Smiths' reconstructive memories, with Rick's written headcount an empirical defense that methodical doubt undermines. Morty's formula that parasites implant only good memories is shown to be merely inductive rather than certain like the cogito, so Beth's shooting of Mr. Poopybutthole becomes the test case: applying Aquinas's three kinds of ignorance, the chapter argues she remains morally responsible despite genuine remorse because she neglected the chance to reconsider Morty's probabilistic rule. The upshot is Descartes's advice to restrain the will beyond what the intellect certifies: shoot for the arm, not the head.

chapters.file: ch23 - III I Have No Code of Ethics, Just Love Killin’.md
ch24 - 12. Jerry’s Dick.md
chapters.relation: Twin essays by two dimension-swapped Wayne Yuens debate whether Jerry owes Shrimply Pibbles his penis in 'Interdimensional Cable 2'. Yuen H-232 defends supererogation: like donating blood or a kidney to a Peter Singer figure, giving up the organ would be Good-Samaritan praiseworthy but beyond duty, since it would derail Jerry's life-plan and autonomy, and the artificial-heart alternative makes it optional, while utilitarianism has no room for such acts. Yuen U-964 replies that the life-plan excuse would absolve every shirked duty up to Evil Morty's massacre of the Citadel, that Singer-style obligation to aid stands, and that in our organ-short world we probably do have a duty to donate.

chapters.file: ch25 - 13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness.md
chapters.relation: The chapter diagnoses Rick's 'Wubba Lubba dub-dub' ('I am in great pain, please help me') as chronic Epicurean suffering and prescribes the tetrapharmakos, the four-part cure. Don't fear the gods: Epicurus's indifferent atomist gods versus Rick's atheism, his panic prayer in 'A Rickle in Time', and Toxic Rick's 'If god exists, it's me' as ego rather than argument. Don't fear death, since 'where death is, I am not', though infinite replacements make Rick and Morty fear each other's death rather than their own. The good is easy to get, so booze, Eyeholes, and Szechuan sauce must yield to water, friends, and family; and the terrible is easy to endure, as when Rick stops resenting Birdperson's wedding and finally turns himself in for his family.

chapters.file: ch26 - 14. Jerryboree!.md
chapters.relation: Arguing that even the interchangeable Jerrys of Jerryboree deserve better, the chapter uses Stephen Darwall's distinction between recognition and appraisal respect: Jerry lacks both, while Rick has appraisal self-respect (he loves his genius) but squanders recognition self-respect by portal-hopping away from every consequence. Jerry's spinelessness is then Sartrean bad faith, from celebrating being 'assigned a function' in 'The Wedding Squanchers' to needing the parasite Sleepy Gary to vouch for his very existence in 'Total Rickall' and lying to Keara in 'The ABCs of Beth'. The chapter closes with Thomas Hill's Kantian case that servility disrespects the moral law in oneself, quoting Kant's worm maxim against Jerry's failed him-or-me ultimatum in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption'.

chapters.file: ch27 - 15. Loving Your Pet Is Better than Utilitarianism.md
chapters.relation: Against Peter Singer's utilitarian case in Animal Liberation, spare Snuffles because he can suffer regardless of intelligence, the chapter argues utilitarianism fails because it quantifies the unquantifiable, happiness. It turns to Hume: intelligence cannot ground moral worth, since smart Rick enslaving a microverse would then be our moral superior; Hume's guillotine separates descriptive from moral claims so that metaphysics no longer decides who counts as a moral object; and Hume's real ground is sentiment, dogs loving across species as the tail-wagging Snuffles does. So the morally right response to 'Lawnmower Dog' is not Jerry's abuse or even Rick's intelligence helmet but simply loving the pet.

chapters.file: ch28 - IV God, Grandpa, You’re Such a Dick!.md
ch29 - 16. He’s Ethickle Rick!!!.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads the Galactic Federation as Hobbes's Sovereign: Earth covenants in for security and gets an interplanetary TSA, pill-currency debt, and the surveillance droid Conroy, while the Citadel of Ricks tours Hobbes's three commonwealths in 'The Ricklantis Mixup', aristocratic Council, brief democracy, and Evil Morty's monarchy, where the Sovereign's rules cannot by definition be unjust. Against this, Rick embodies Hobbes's psychological egoism ('the object to every man is his own pleasure'), hiding his motives in the Riq IV hostage gambit and the Szechuan-sauce confession. Yet the chapter argues Rick's egoism is oddly ethical: in an infinite multiverse resources are not scarce, so refusing to surrender freedom to any Sovereign and competing for everything is the right way to live, with 'A Rickle in Time' and the self-sacrifice of 'The Wedding Squanchers' as its tested limits.

chapters.file: ch30 - 17. Who Is “Rick” Anyway.md
chapters.relation: Starting from the mangled sentence 'Rick is the Rickest Rick who ever Ricked', the chapter asks what the name 'Rick' refers to in a multiverse. It contrasts Saul Kripke's view, names rigidly designate the same person across imagined counterfactuals, which would absurdly make the Council of Ricks one many-located Rick, with David Lewis's counterpart theory, each possibility a real world of world-bound duplicates. The show sides with Lewis: the Council says 'Rick C-137', C-137 works like a distinguishing last name, and Morty's 'I eat breakfast twenty yards away from my own rotting corpse' in 'Rixty Minutes' is true only because the corpse belongs to a Morty just like him. The chapter ends by noting Lewis never handled inter-reality travel, so which Summer C-137 Morty now refers to remains open.

chapters.file: ch31 - 18. What Makes Rick Tick.md
chapters.relation: Surveying Rick's values area by area, a many-worlds multiverse, atheism ('There is no God, Summer'), scientism, egoistic ethics, hatred of all government, and rap as today's Romanticism, the chapter rejects absurdism, existentialism, nihilism, and even Max Stirner's individualist anarchism, which it says fits the Citadel of Ricks rather than the loner Rick. Its thesis is that Rick is an Ayn Rand Objectivist: Rand's ideal man of reason, independence, and rejection of altruism, collectivism, and mysticism, with Jerry as the pity-parasite anti-ideal exposed in 'The Whirly Dirly Conspiracy'. It warns that infinite choice risks the paradox of hedonism, pointing to Rick's half-hearted suicide machine after Unity, and ends that only chosen constructive goals, perhaps a kinder Rick, could save him, if some other universe didn't already have that Rick.

chapters.file: ch32 - 19. The Citadel of Ricks Is Untruth.md
chapters.relation: The chapter reads Rick C-137's war on the Citadel through Kierkegaard's claim that the crowd is untruth: the Council of Ricks is the leveling public, envying and punishing the passionate individual ('You're a rogue Rick, irrational, passionate'), as Rick J-22's breakdown over Simple Rick's wafers in 'The Ricklantis Mixup' dramatizes, while our Rick stays himself by refusing consensus. From Philosophical Fragments, via Socrates's maieutic midwifery, it draws Kierkegaard's ethics of selfhood: one person can only be the occasion for another's self-knowledge and must then push them away to become individuals. That is exactly Rick's advice to Beth in 'The ABCs of Beth', to leave Jerry, saddle her universe, and become herself, since only Beth can make Beth.

chapters.file: ch33 - 20. Getting Your Shit Together Stoic Style.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Rick is at his best an Epictetus-style Stoic: in 'A Rickle in Time' his total certainty keeps the split timelines perfectly synced, enacting 'choice alone is vice, choice alone is virtue'; his 'love is a chemical reaction... focus on science' speech in 'Rick Potion #9' treats passion as an impression outside the sphere of control; and his 'don't think about it' dismissal of the Hitler-cured-cancer reality applies the dichotomy of control to an unmasterable multiverse. Epictetus's model of hardship as training is vindicated by Cronenberged Jerry, whose struggle preserves his dignity in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption', and the chapter closes with the Stoic promise Rick's life shows: not pleasure but contentment.

holes.name: Intrinsic vs Instrumental Value
holes.what: Something has intrinsic value when it is valued for what it is in itself, and instrumental value when valued only as a means to something else.
holes.why: Chapter 1 ('The Genuine Article') is organized entirely around whether genuine Beth, reality itself, and happiness are intrinsically or merely instrumentally valuable, and no taxonomy slug covers the distinction.

holes.name: Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence
holes.what: A theory is underdetermined when the available evidence could equally well support rival theories, so no observation can decide between them.
holes.why: Chapter 3 makes the 'devastating' epistemological problem that every possible piece of evidence for the simulation hypothesis equally supports its denial the centerpiece of its skepticism.

holes.name: Correspondence and Coherence Theories of Truth
holes.what: The correspondence theory says a claim is true when it matches an actual state of the world; the coherence theory says truth is consistency with all other true claims.
holes.why: Chapter 6 ('Truth in a Multiverse') builds its whole account of what makes claims true across timelines on this correspondence/coherence distinction, which taxonomy lacks, having only James's pragmatic truth.

holes.name: Confirmation Bias and Dual-Process Thinking
holes.what: The tendency to seek and favor evidence confirming existing beliefs, driven by fast automatic System 1 thinking over slow deliberate System 2 reasoning (Kahneman, Wason).
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire analysis of the Headism religion in 'Get Schwifty' rests on illusory correlation, confirmation bias, and System 1/System 2 cognition, none of which taxonomy covers.

holes.name: Aquinas on Ignorance and Moral Responsibility
holes.what: Aquinas's distinction between concomitant, feigned or negligent, and consequent ignorance, which determines when ignorance excuses an action from moral responsibility.
holes.why: Chapter 11 uses the three kinds of ignorance to decide whether Beth is morally responsible for shooting Mr. Poopybutthole, a doctrine taxonomy lacks among its Aquinas entries.

holes.name: Supererogation (acts beyond duty)
holes.what: Supererogatory acts are praiseworthy deeds that go beyond moral obligation, so that declining them is not wrong, a category utilitarianism refuses to recognize.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire two-part debate over whether Jerry must give Shrimply Pibbles his penis, and by extension whether we must donate kidneys and blood, turns on the obligatory/supererogatory line.

holes.name: Self-Respect (recognition vs appraisal; servility)
holes.what: Recognition self-respect is the regard owed to oneself as a rational autonomous agent, appraisal self-respect is earned for one's traits, and its absence is servility (Darwall, Hill).
holes.why: Chapter 14's diagnosis of Jerry, and its contrast with Rick's portal-assisted irresponsibility, is built on Darwall's two kinds of self-respect and Hill on servility, which kant-respect alone does not capture.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century novelist-philosopher whose Objectivism (rational egoism) holds rational self-interest as the highest virtue, rejecting altruism, collectivism, and mysticism.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire thesis is that Rick is an Objectivist in Rand's sense, her 'ideal man', and taxonomy has no entry for Rand or Objectivism.

holes.name: Max Stirner
holes.what: Nineteenth-century German egoist anarchist who held that only one's own interest and ability limit action, with egoists free to form loose unions of mutual need.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Stirner's individualist anarchism to distinguish the loner Rick from the Citadel of Ricks, which the chapter says Stirner's union of egoists actually describes.

holes.name: The Crowd Is Untruth (the public and leveling)
holes.what: Kierkegaard's critique of 'the public' as an abstraction in which the crowd becomes untruth, leveling individuals through envy, gossip, and passionless inaction.
holes.why: Chapter 19's whole reading of the Citadel of Ricks as envy, leveling, and passionlessness rests on this Kierkegaardian concept, which taxonomy lacks.
